text:
Not recommended for anything sensitive. It works, but it is the weakest common option.

**Any JavaScript running on your page can read localStorage, so a single XSS bug lets an attacker copy the token and use it from their own machine until it expires.** This includes an injected script, a compromised npm dependency, or a third-party analytics tag. An httpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, so XSS can still act inside the victim's open tab but cannot take the token elsewhere.

| | localStorage | httpOnly cookie | memory + httpOnly refresh cookie |
|---|---|---|---|
| XSS steals token | yes | no | access token only, short-lived |
| CSRF exposure | none | yes, needs `SameSite` + CSRF token | refresh endpoint only |
| survives reload | yes | yes | yes, via silent refresh |
| cross-domain API | easy | needs CORS `credentials` + same site | same |
| effort | lowest | low | medium |

pick: httpOnly cookie with `Secure; SameSite=Lax|Strict` for same-site apps. Use access token in memory plus an httpOnly refresh cookie when the SPA and API sit on different origins or need `Authorization` headers.

localStorage is acceptable when all of these hold:
- the token is short-lived, ≈ 5-15 min
- the token can be revoked server-side
- a strict CSP blocks inline and third-party scripts
- the app holds low-value data

Cookies do not fix XSS. They only stop the token from being stolen. XSS prevention (output escaping, CSP, dependency hygiene) is still the main defense.
